cards.title: Can making everyone equally worse off ever be an improvement?
cards.body: If equality is intrinsically good, then blinding every sighted person makes the world fairer. Philosopher Derek Parfit called this the "leveling down objection." It exposes a troubling flaw in strict egalitarianism: if closing the gap is all that matters, destroying advantages without helping the disadvantaged counts as progress. To escape this absurdity, many ethicists shifted to "prioritarianism," arguing our duty is to benefit the worst off, not drag everyone down to equal misery.

cards.title: Why is life-giving water cheap while useless diamonds cost a fortune?
cards.body: Water is essential for human survival, yet it costs pennies. Diamonds are decorative luxuries, yet they cost thousands. In 1776, Adam Smith highlighted this "diamond-water paradox." The puzzle remained unsolved until nineteenth-century thinkers introduced marginal utility: humans evaluate goods not by their total usefulness to humanity, but by the value of the next single unit. Because water is abundant, an extra cup satisfies a minor urge; because diamonds are scarce, the next diamond satisfies a rare desire.

cards.title: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure
cards.body: In 1975, British economist Charles Goodhart observed that the moment a government targets a financial metric to control the economy, the metric's reliability collapses. Known as Goodhart's Law, this principle governs all human systems. When schools evaluate teachers solely by standardized test scores, teachers begin teaching to the test or inflating grades. By optimizing for the number that represents quality, people systematically distort and undermine the very quality the number was meant to track.

cards.title: Cantor's math proved that an all-knowing mind is logically impossible
cards.body: Can anyone know everything? In 1991, philosopher Patrick Grim used Georg Cantor's set theory to show that omniscience is logically impossible. An all-knowing mind would need to grasp the set of all truths. But Cantor proved that the collection of subsets for any set is always strictly larger than the original set. This means any supposed "total list of truths" generates even more new truths about its combinations, leaving reality infinitely larger than any single mind could contain.

cards.title: The ancient puzzle of how we can talk about things that don't exist
cards.body: If you say "Pegasus does not exist," what are you talking about? If Pegasus is truly nothing, your sentence has no subject; but if Pegasus is something you can mention, it seems to possess some form of existence. In 1948, philosopher Willard Van Orman Quine nicknamed this "Plato's beard"—a tangled metaphysical problem that tangled logic for centuries. Modern logic shaved it by showing that names like Pegasus are shorthand descriptions, not real-world entities awaiting a tag.

quizzes.question: What does Derek Parfit's "leveling down objection" demonstrate about strict egalitarianism?
options: Blindly pursuing equality can treat harming the advantaged as moral progress
Total equality is mathematically impossible in a modern market economy
Unequal societies always generate more technological innovation
Prioritizing the worst off requires eliminating all personal property
quizzes.explanation: The leveling down objection argues that if inequality itself is the sole evil, destroying advantages without helping anyone would perversely count as an improvement.

quizzes.question: How does modern economics solve Adam Smith's diamond-water paradox?
options: Through marginal utility, which values the next available unit rather than total necessity
By calculating the physical energy required to mine diamonds versus extract water
Through government subsidies that artificially suppress the price of drinking water
By demonstrating that water holds no subjective economic value to consumers
quizzes.explanation: Marginal utility explains that abundant goods have low value for the next extra unit, whereas scarce goods like diamonds command high value per additional unit.

quizzes.question: What core principle is summarized by Goodhart's Law?
options: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
Bad money inevitably drives good money out of general circulation
Complex bureaucratic systems inevitably expand to fill available working hours
A system's overall reliability is determined entirely by its weakest component
quizzes.explanation: Goodhart's Law states that optimizing directly for a performance metric causes people to game or distort the metric, ruining its ability to measure quality.

quizzes.question: Why did philosopher Patrick Grim conclude that absolute omniscience is impossible?
options: Cantor's theorem shows any set of truths generates a strictly larger set of new truths
Quantum mechanics proves that the act of observing alters physical reality
Conscious observers cannot mathematically formulate statements about themselves
Human language lacks sufficient vocabulary to name an infinite number of facts
quizzes.explanation: Patrick Grim applied Cantor's power set theorem to show that there cannot exist a complete "set of all truths," as power sets generate new truths indefinitely.

quizzes.question: What logical dilemma does the philosophical phrase "Plato's beard" describe?
options: Denying the existence of something seems to require that it exist in order to be named
Knowing that you know nothing creates an endless skeptical regress
Abstract mathematical shapes cannot exist without an ideal world of forms
Socratic questioning inevitably traps all philosophical definitions in circles
quizzes.explanation: "Plato's beard" refers to the paradox of non-existence: stating that something does not exist seems to require that thing to be "something" in order to talk about it.

misconceptions.claim: Strict egalitarianism only aims to lift up the poor, never pull down the wealthy.
misconceptions.explanation: Parfit's leveling down objection shows that pure egalitarianism values closing gaps, meaning making the rich poorer counts as a fairer world even if the poor gain nothing.

misconceptions.claim: The market price of a resource reflects how essential it is to human life.
misconceptions.explanation: The diamond-water paradox shows prices reflect marginal utility and relative scarcity, not an item's biological importance.

misconceptions.claim: Tying employee bonuses to a precise numerical metric guarantees higher genuine quality.
misconceptions.explanation: Goodhart's Law demonstrates that when a metric becomes the target, people optimize for the number itself, often undermining genuine quality.

misconceptions.claim: Mathematical set theory implies that no mind can possess a complete set of all truths.
misconceptions.explanation: Patrick Grim demonstrated that by Cantor's power set theorem, any supposed set of all truths generates strictly more truths, making a closed set of all knowledge impossible.
